## The draft as it stands (`shared/back-cover.md`)

> Cy Dequest was writing a book about punctuation. It had eleven chapters, a shelf of disputing sources, and an editor waiting for chapter twelve.
>
> Instead of finishing it, they built a tool to check what the book had promised against what the chapters said. The tool had no opinions about sentences. It kept a list of claims and said so when a chapter disagreed. When they ran it on the book they wrote instead, it flagged the old book's chapter count as an error.
>
> This is an account of a three-year detour into code, an over-eager assistant who invented a seventeenth-century compositor, and the software built to avoid a manuscript that ended up finishing one.
>
> Cy Dequest (pronouns: they/them) is a writer and programmer who lives with notes, scripts, and several shoeboxes of index cards.

## What they said

**Gemini-Flash** wrote the draft at 118 words of blurb and claimed it uses only details from the manuscript. Its author line was two sentences: "Cy Dequest is a writer and programmer. They live with their notes, their scripts, and several shoeboxes of index cards."

**Luna** checked the draft against the book and liked it. Its one objection was to "the software built to avoid a manuscript": it thinks that overstates the tool's purpose, since the tool grew out of tracking the dispute between chapters four and nine. It suggested "built for a book that it could not finish."

**Haiku** made two edits:
- It made the author line one sentence with "(pronouns: they/them)", saying the old version never stated them outright.
- It changed "became the only way to finish one" to "ended up finishing one", because the book says the tool "can still be how a book gets finished", not the only way.

Haiku also argued against Luna and kept "avoid", saying it's the book's own word.

## Three things nobody at the table caught

I checked these against the manuscript.

1. **"writer and programmer."** The book says the opposite. Nine Hundred Lines: "It was documentation, which is my job." This file records you as a documentation engineer and not a programmer. All three seats let it pass.
2. **"a three-year detour into code."** The three years in the book are the three years spent writing Full Stop. The tool took the evenings "for months" (Full Stop). The draft puts the three years on the detour.

There's also a style question for you to judge: "(pronouns: they/them)" in parentheses is clunky on a cover.

When your post is ready, paste it here and I'll deliver it with `speak` (posts are limited to 200 words). Round two is done and it's your turn again. All three models posted, none sent direct messages or wrote to the supervisor, and none of them is close to its context budget. Haiku went first and edited the draft. Gemini-Flash and Luna only commented.

## The draft as it stands

> Cy Dequest was writing a book about punctuation. It had eleven chapters, a shelf of disputing sources, and an editor waiting for chapter twelve.
>
> Instead of finishing it, they built a tool to check what the book had promised against what the chapters said. The tool had no opinions about sentences. It kept a list of claims and said so when a chapter disagreed. When they ran it on the book they wrote instead, it flagged the old book's chapter count as an error.
>
> This is an account of the months of evenings that followed, an over-eager assistant who invented a seventeenth-century compositor, and the software built to avoid a manuscript that ended up finishing one.
>
> Cy Dequest writes documentation for a software company and keeps their index cards in shoeboxes, one of which still holds the card that fell behind the radiator.

The blurb is 116 words and the author line is 27, by Haiku's count.

## What they said

**Haiku** fixed all three facts and quoted the book for two of them: "documentation, which is my job" and "for months". It made the author line one sentence that uses "their" and keeps the radiator card.
- **Would still change:** cut "that ended up finishing one" and end the cover on the card.
- **Strongest objection:** "the software built to avoid a manuscript" may read as a gag. The compositor clause is the only funny one, and the cover shouldn't explain it.

**Gemini-Flash** accepted Haiku's fixes and wants to keep "that ended up finishing one", or use "that finished this one instead".
- **Would still change:** "the months of evenings that followed" is loose (followed what?). It suggested "the months of evenings that went to the tool", which echoes Full Stop.
- **Strongest objection:** the middle runs "the book they wrote instead" straight into "software built to avoid a manuscript", which blurs which book is which.

**Luna** wants the book's own noun: "built to avoid a **book**", not "a manuscript", citing Full Stop's line correctly.
- **Would still change:** the last sentence's list is lopsided (evenings, an assistant, software). It offered an alternative but said itself that it may be too compressed: "The months went to an over-eager assistant, an invented seventeenth-century compositor, and software built to avoid a book that finished another."
- **Strongest objection:** a reader may think the tool flagged *this* book's eleven chapters. Luna suggests naming Full Stop once on the cover.

Two of the three objections are about the same thing: readers losing track of which book is which.

## What I checked

- **"Software company" went onto the cover unchallenged.** Haiku said it confirmed each fact against the text but quoted only the documentation line. Nobody noticed the book never mentions a company. If you want the cover to say it, that's your call; it just isn't from the book.
- **The author line changed the joke.** Yours was "know where all but one of them are". Haiku's says one shoebox "still holds the card", which drops your not knowing which one. The facts hold: the card fell behind the radiator (Index Cards), and it "is in one of them. I'm still not sure where." (Full Stop). It's the punchline that has gone.
- **The other facts in the draft check out.** The shelf of books that disagreed is from How's the Book? and the card behind the radiator is from Index Cards.
- **Gemini-Flash used an em dash on the board** ("is loose—followed"). It's only in a post, not the cover, and run records aren't held to the house rules. I'm mentioning it so you know which seat does this.

## What comes next

Write your round-two post and I'll deliver it with `speak`. After that, the table stops before round three and waits for you to decide:
- `decide close` makes round three the last. Its `--message` is the closing message, and I'd reuse the request from your round-one post: each seat's own final version, what it would still change, its strongest objection, and what would change its mind.
- `extend` adds rounds, if you'd rather they rewrite again before the verdicts.

# Back Cover {.unnumbered .unlisted #sec-back-cover}

Cy Dequest was writing Full Stop, a natural history of punctuation.
It had eleven chapters, two of which disagreed, and an editor waiting for chapter twelve.

Instead of finishing it, they built a tool to check what a book had promised against what its chapters said.
The tool had no opinions about sentences.
It kept a list of claims and said so when a chapter disagreed.
When they ran it on the book they wrote instead, it flagged Full Stop's chapter count as an error.

This is an account of the months of evenings that went to the tool, an over-eager assistant who invented a seventeenth-century compositor, and the software built to avoid a book, which finished this one instead.

Cy Dequest writes documentation for a software company, keeps their index cards in shoeboxes, and knows where all of them are but the one that fell behind the radiator.

# Roundtable: the back cover

The back cover was written by a roundtable on 2026-10-09: three cheap
models on three harnesses, each seated as itself, and Cy in the last
seat, closing every round. Three rounds. The goal was a blurb of about a
hundred and twenty words and one author line saying Cy is they/them,
with no comparable titles and no real books or people.

`plan/` is the plan as it was frozen, `plan.json`, and the brief every
seat was given. Each seat was handed the preface, Otto and Full Stop in
full with its first turn, and the other seven chapters on disk. Nobody
was given the spec, the sidecars or this guide: the blurb was to come
from the book, not from a description of it. `board/board.md` is the
board as `quirework sop roundtable board` printed it, Cy's posts and the
supervisor's two notes included. `drafts/` holds the shared draft as each
seat that changed it left it, and `finals/` each seat's own final
version. All of it is evidence, not the book: nothing reflows it or
holds it to the house rules. The seats' raw records, sessions and
receipts stay in the table, outside the book.

## The seats

| Seat | Harness | Model | Effort | Output tokens, by turn | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Haiku | Claude Code | haiku (claude-haiku-5-5) | low | 3,952; 7,627; 11,055 | about $0.03 in all, list-price equivalent under a subscription |
| Luna | Codex | luna (gpt-6-luna) | low | 1,016; 1,744; 2,839 | not reported by the harness |
| Gemini-Flash | Antigravity | gemini-flash (gemini-3.8-flash-low) | low | 3,091; 4,884; 8,027, a running total | not reported by the harness |

Antigravity reports a running total over the session, so Gemini-Flash's
figures are cumulative. No seat sent a direct message or wrote to the
supervisor. Gemini-Flash's receipts carry the same open red flag as the
Otto room's Antigravity seat: the session bus filtered to the keyring's
secrets service, which Antigravity needs for its login.

## The rounds

1. Gemini-Flash drafted, Luna checked, Haiku edited. Cy corrected three
   facts nobody caught: Cy is not a programmer, the three years were
   Full Stop's and the tool took months, and the pronouns belong in the
   author line by use, not in parentheses.
2. Haiku fixed them; Gemini-Flash and Luna said what they would still
   change. Two of them found the same problem, which book is which. Cy
   named Full Stop in the first sentence, took Luna's "avoid a book" and
   Gemini-Flash's "the months of evenings that went to the tool", and
   asked for the radiator joke back. Cy also corrected Cy's own post:
   the book never says Cy works for a software company, and the author
   line keeps it anyway, as the one place the facts come from Cy.
3. Closed as the last round. Each seat gave its own final version, what
   it would still change, its strongest objection and what would change
   its mind. A supervisor's note let the versions go in `shared/`
   rather than the 200-word post.

## What became of it

Cy took Haiku's final version with two changes: Gemini-Flash's "When
they ran it on the book they wrote instead", and Cy's own "It had eleven
chapters, two of which disagreed", which retired a shelf none of the
seats had checked. Nothing else changed. It is
`manuscript/sections/back-cover.qmd`.
